fixes.title: Add the proof personas asked for
fixes.why: What would make them star: "A short comparison section showing why this beats JWT / Django signing / raw hmac (key rotation, max_age expiry, algorithm choices), an explicit note that data is signed but NOT encrypted, and proof of maturity such as who depends on it, release history, or a security model/threat description."; "A short plain-English line right under the example saying: 'This signs data, it does not hide it (anyone can read the token, but nobody can change it without the key)', plus a tiny real use, such as a 5-line password-reset link with try/except BadSignature, so I know exactly when I would use it."; "Show proof of maturity above the fold: state the license in text (e.g. BSD/MIT), last release date and maintainer or org, a line on who uses it, and one sentence on how it differs from JWT and that it signs but does not encrypt (plus expiry support)."

truth.purpose: A Python library that cryptographically signs (HMAC) serialized data so it can be sent through untrusted places such as cookies, URLs or emailed links, and verified as untampered (optionally not expired) when it comes back.
truth.audience: Python web developers who need tamper-proof tokens, e.g. for sessions, password-reset or account-activation links.
derived_from: repo tree (src/itsdangerous: signer, serializer, timed, url_safe)

response.what_it_does: A Python library that cryptographically signs data with a secret key so you can put it in a cookie, URL or emailed link and detect on return whether it was tampered with.
response.who_its_for: Python web developers (Flask-style apps) who need signed cookies, password-reset links, email confirmation tokens, or similar tamper-evident tokens without rolling their own.
confusions: How is this different from JWT / PyJWT, Django's signing module, or just using hmac directly? The README doesn't say.
Is the payload encrypted or only signed? The example token is JSON, so I assume readable, but it isn't stated and a careless user could put secrets in it.
What are the security guarantees: which algorithm (HMAC-SHA1? SHA256?), key rotation support, expiry/timestamps, replay protection? Nothing above the fold.
What does 'salt' actually do here and when do I need it?
The badges are just names with no visible status, so I can't tell whether the tests pass or how mature or maintained it is.
No indication of who uses it, how old it is, or whether it is audited, so I can't tell if it's a weekend project or battle-tested.
response.would_make_me_star: A short comparison section showing why this beats JWT / Django signing / raw hmac (key rotation, max_age expiry, algorithm choices), an explicit note that data is signed but NOT encrypted, and proof of maturity such as who depends on it, release history, or a security model/threat description.

grade.notes: Exact. Still asks for JWT comparison and signed-vs-encrypted: both exist, but just below the fold.

response.what_it_does: It lets you put a secret-key signature on some data (like a user id) so that if you give it to someone else, like in a cookie or a link, you can tell if they changed it when it comes back.
response.who_its_for: Python developers building web things like logins, cookies, or emailed links; probably people who already know a bit about web apps.
confusions: What exactly is a 'salt' and why is it set to 'auth'? Not explained.
What is a 'serializer' and what do dumps/loads do? I only guess from the example.
Does this encrypt the data or only sign it? Can someone read the token? The text doesn't say.
What is the 'secret key' supposed to be in real use, and where do I keep it? 'secret key' in the example looks like a placeholder.
Does it work on its own or only with a web framework? I can't tell from this part.
What do the 'Tests' and 'License' badges say? I can't see status or version, so I can't tell if it's maintained.
Why is the name 'ItsDangerous'? Is it risky to use? A bit scary for a beginner.
The comment 'raises BadSignature' is shown but the example doesn't show how to handle it (try/except) even though BadSignature is imported.
response.would_make_me_star: A short plain-English line right under the example saying: 'This signs data, it does not hide it (anyone can read the token, but nobody can change it without the key)', plus a tiny real use, such as a 5-line password-reset link with try/except BadSignature, so I know exactly when I would use it.
